evidence.claim: Kansas’s Historic Route 66 Byway crosses the state’s southeastern corner on 13 miles of town streets and older highway.
evidence.quote: Driving Directions Distance: 13 miles

evidence.claim: Kansas Tourism places it at the edge of the Ozarks and highlights mining history, the Rainbow Bridge and connections to the film Cars.
evidence.quote: This scenic corner is where the Ozarks spill into the State.

evidence.claim: The route links Baxter Springs, Riverton and Galena, with a crossing of Brush Creek west of Riverton.
evidence.quote: It passes through Baxter Springs, Riverton and Galena in Cherokee County.

evidence.claim: At the creek, the narrow concrete arch survives beside its replacement.
evidence.quote: The bridge is fairly narrow, and due to traffic on the road, a replacement bridge has been built.

evidence.claim: on 13 miles of town streets and older highway.
evidence.quote: while driving the original Kansas portion of Route 66

evidence.claim: highlights mining history, the Rainbow Bridge and connections to the film Cars.
evidence.quote: Meet your favorite characters from Pixar’s “Cars” franchise, dig deep into the mining history of the area, take a photo on the last remaining ‘ Rainbow Bridge ’ along the route

evidence.claim: with a crossing of Brush Creek west of Riverton.
evidence.quote: The Rainbow Bridge is an old bridge over Brush Creek approximately two miles west of Riverton, Kansas

evidence.claim: Route 66 received its number in 1926, and Kansas paved its section in 1929.
evidence.quote: US Route 66 was designated in 1926; by 1929 Kansas and Illinois were the first to completely pave their respective segments of this highway.

evidence.claim: Interstate 44 changed the journey in 1961: it crossed directly from Oklahoma to Missouri, missing Kansas by a quarter mile.
evidence.quote: the new Interstate highway crossed directly from Oklahoma to Missouri, bypassing Kansas entirely by just a quarter mile (400 m).

evidence.claim: The loss of highway traffic, together with lead and zinc mine closures, contributed to the closure of many Cherokee County businesses.
evidence.quote: lead and zinc mine closures in the Tri-State district plus the diversion of US 66 traffic by I-44 led to the closure of many local Cherokee County businesses.

evidence.claim: After US 66 was decommissioned in 1985, its final Kansas alignment became US 69 Alternate and K-66.
evidence.quote: US-69 Alternate was formed in 1985 when US-66 was decommissioned; the remainder of US-66 in Kansas became K-66.

evidence.claim: Interstate 44 changed the journey in 1961
evidence.quote: When US 66 was bypassed by Interstate 44 (I-44) in 1961

evidence.claim: From the Oklahoma line, head north on Military Avenue through Baxter Springs.
evidence.quote: At the Kansas-Oklahoma border, travel north on K-66 (also known as Military Ave/U.S. 69Alt) to Baxter Springs.

evidence.claim: The byway turns west at Third Street, follows Willow Avenue and 50th Street toward Rainbow Bridge, then turns east toward Riverton.
evidence.quote: At 3rd St, turn west to continue on K-66 (also known as Willow Ave and 50th St.). At the Marsh Arch "Rainbow" Bridge, take Beasley Rd/K-66 east

evidence.claim: K-66 continues to Galena, where Main Street, Front Street and State Line Road lead to the Missouri endpoint.
evidence.quote: Stay on K-66 into Riverton and beyond where the road becomes 7th St/K-66. In Galena, take Main St north to Front St. Continue east on Front St, then take State Line Rd south to the byway’s end at Missouri Hwy 66.

evidence.claim: Rainbow Bridge carried traffic over Brush Creek before Route 66 had its number.
evidence.quote: It was built in 1923.

evidence.claim: Built in 1923, it is a single-span concrete Marsh arch, the only surviving bridge of that type along the former highway.
evidence.quote: The bridge is a single-span concrete Marsh arch bridge and is the sole surviving bridge of this type on the entire length of the former highway.

evidence.claim: Kansas Route 66 once had two more Marsh arches, both crossing the Spring River.
evidence.quote: Two other Marsh arch bridges were also located on US 66 in Kansas, both over the Spring River.

evidence.claim: A replacement crossing now handles the main road, while the old bridge survives on a short one-way branch.
evidence.quote: The road curves toward the new bridge toward Baxter Springs, but a short, one-way road carries traffic to the Rainbow Bridge, which may still be crossed.

evidence.claim: Its National Register name is Brush Creek Bridge, recognizing its connection with US 66.
evidence.quote: The bridge has been placed on the National Register of Historic Places (as the Brush Creek Bridge) on March 10, 1983, due to its connection with US-66

evidence.claim: A single concrete Marsh arch spans Brush Creek beside the replacement crossing.
evidence.quote: The bridge is a single-span concrete Marsh arch bridge

evidence.claim: Riverton’s historic Williams’ Store predates Route 66 by a year.
evidence.quote: Leo Williams built the store in 1925, the year before Route 66 was designated.

evidence.claim: Leo Williams built it in 1925, and he and his wife Lora sold groceries, general merchandise, chili and barbecue beef to travelers.
evidence.quote: While it was mainly a grocery and general store, Williams and his wife Lora sold chili and barbecue beef to travelers on Route 66.

evidence.claim: A croquet court hosted local tournaments before it gave way to parking.
evidence.quote: The store even had a croquet court at one point, which hosted local tournaments. The court was eventually removed to add parking.

evidence.claim: Later known as the Eisler Brothers store, it was a stop on Pixar’s research trips for Cars.
evidence.quote: The Eisler Brothers Country Store in Riverton was one of the stops on Pixar's US 66 research trips for the 2006 film Cars.

evidence.claim: There, filmmakers met Dean Walker, whose ability to turn his feet backward and walk in reverse became one of many inspirations for Mater.
evidence.quote: The filmmakers met with Dean Walker, then president of the Kansas Historic Route 66 Association, who is known to twist his feet backwards 180° and walk in reverse. He became one of many inspirations for the Mater character

evidence.claim: Later known as the Eisler Brothers store
evidence.quote: The store is now known as the Eisler Brothers Old Riverton Store.

evidence.claim: Galena took its name from the lead ore discovered here in 1877.
evidence.quote: taking the present name of Galena in 1877, which is named after the lead ore galena found in the area.

evidence.claim: A railroad had already arrived in 1871, but the community began after the lead discovery.
evidence.quote: Although the railroad was built through the territory of Galena in 1871, the community did not start until the discovery of lead there in the spring of 1877.

evidence.claim: Route 66 later brought another kind of traffic to Main Street, where the Kan-O-Tex station served motorists in 1934.
evidence.quote: The Kan-O-Tex Service Station in Galena, Kansas, United States is a Kan-O-Tex filling station that originally served U.S. Route 66 motorists in 1934.

evidence.claim: After years of vacancy, the station was restored in 2007.
evidence.quote: the station sat vacant, closed and largely abandoned until its 2007 restoration.

evidence.claim: Its 1951 International boom truck helped inspire Pixar’s Tow Mater.
evidence.quote: The station is home to a 1951 International boom truck on which Pixar's animated character Tow Mater was based

evidence.claim: The truck is named Tater; the restored station retains the original design of its pumps and exterior.
evidence.quote: the original truck has been named "Tater."

evidence.claim: the restored station retains the original design of its pumps and exterior.
evidence.quote: the station retains the original aesthetic design of the fuel pumps and exterior façade

evidence.claim: It entered the National Register in 1983, six decades after its construction.
evidence.quote: on March 10, 1983, due to its connection with US-66

evidence.claim: The store entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2003.
evidence.quote: The store was added to the National Register of Historic Places on August 29, 2003.

evidence.claim: The Kan-O-Tex name combined Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas, giving the regional fuel brand its name.
evidence.quote: a now-defunct regional fuel brand named for Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.

flags: The current “first state” paving claim is inconsistent across 18 (Kansas first) and 07 (Kansas and Illinois first); retain 1929 without priority. The current Galena population claim is present in 04 but lacks a dated basis and is omitted as unnecessary precision.

Use Kansas Tourism’s 13-mile historic byway and Oklahoma-to-Missouri driving order, matching strip miles. Cache 18 distinguishes the final numbered highway alignment but internally disagrees on the date of the Galena rerouting; omit that date.

Rainbow Bridge’s one-way branch is described, but the cache lacks a current road-manager access notice or travel direction for the branch. Do not infer a northbound bridge crossing from the overall itinerary. No dated practical instruction is supplied.

All current moments and their coordinates and motifs retained. Riverton’s store is itself a documented historic landmark (09), not an unrelated business substitution. The cache gives little terrain detail beyond the Ozark setting and creek crossing; driving time is not established.
